assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal approach to the open economy (the Redux model and Foundations of International Macroeconomics) reshaped how international macroeconomics is done. It underpins modern open-economy policy models with nominal rigidities. The exchange-rate disconnect and PPP puzzles are a durable empirical agenda. The impact on both theory and policy analysis is broad.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the two clear architects of the framework, through joint papers and the 1996 textbook. Two names is a compact, defensible attribution. Rogoff's separate crisis-history work (B007) is not needed to justify this award.
assessment.maturity: Core contributions date from the mid-1990s to about 2000 and are thoroughly confirmed. They have been absorbed into central-bank and IMF modeling practice. Timing is long overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Some may view the contribution as a synthesis of existing intertemporal and New Keynesian ideas rather than a single discovery.
The disconnect puzzles are still not resolved, so the empirical side of the credit is open.
The committee may prefer a different international macro or finance-oriented award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work changed the understanding of how technology and trade reallocate labor demand and wages. It covers the task-based view of automation, the skill-premium race between education and technology, and local labor-market effects of import competition. It has had very large influence on research and public debate, and the empirical designs are widely emulated.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across several authors. Katz is tied to the education-technology race and the skill premium, Autor to the task approach and the China shock, and Hanson to the China shock and local adjustment. Dorn is a co-author of the China shock work, and Acemoglu (a 2024 laureate) and Levy-Murnane are important to the task framework but not listed. Three names capture the central empirical contributions but leave out meaningful contributors.
assessment.maturity: The skill-premium work dates from the early 1990s and the China shock from 2013. The empirical findings have been tested and partly qualified. Long-run welfare and adjustment conclusions are still being debated.
uncertainties: Contested attribution among Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz and uncredited task-framework authors.
The size and persistence of trade-shock effects remain debated.
Overlap with the 2024 prize on technology and institutions may matter little, but it is a consideration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work covers the political economy of trade policy (Grossman-Helpman 'Protection for Sale'). It also covers the endogenous-growth and trade synthesis (Innovation and Growth in the Global Economy), which is directly relevant to growth theory. Together these are foundational contributions to modern trade and growth theory, with continuing influence.
assessment.attribution: Grossman and Helpman are a natural pair, with an unusually long and productive collaboration and a shared book and papers. Helpman also appears in B008, so the committee would have to avoid crediting him twice. Redding and Melitz are not part of this attribution.
assessment.maturity: Contributions date from the 1990s and are thoroughly established and widely applied. Empirical testing of protection-for-sale is mixed but has been productive.
uncertainties: Empirical support for the political-economy model of protection is mixed.
Helpman's overlap with the firm-heterogeneity candidate could split support.
The committee may prefer to recognize the firm-heterogeneity trade revolution instead.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) 'Credit Cycles' is a foundational model of how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It underlies much of macro-finance and the post-2008 modeling of financial frictions. The contribution is a clean, general mechanism that has been used extensively.
assessment.attribution: The credit-cycle mechanism is tied to Kiyotaki and Moore, who developed it together, and Moore's earlier work with Hart on debt and incomplete contracts supports it. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and empirical frictions, but their work is closer to Bernanke's already recognized contribution. Two names give the sharpest attribution.
assessment.maturity: The contribution dates from 1997 and has had many years of confirmation, extension and use in policy models. The 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig partly covers adjacent ground.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises.
Whether the committee would credit Gertler or Gilchrist in addition.
The empirical validation of the collateral-constraint mechanism is less clean than its theoretical impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Staggered nominal pricing, interest-rate rules and the microfounded New Keynesian framework form the basis of modern monetary-policy analysis and of central-bank DSGE models. The contribution is of very high practical and scientific importance.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest attribution on the list. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the unifying framework) are the most distinct. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims on the quantitative empirical side. Any three-name selection will leave out major contributors, which weakens its prospects of consensus.
assessment.maturity: The ideas date from the 1980s to the early 2000s and have decades of confirmation and use. The framework has been challenged and revised since 2008 and since the recent inflation episode, and heterogeneous-agent extensions are now prominent.
uncertainties: Highly diffuse credit across many candidates.
Whether the framework's structure or its empirical implementations deserve the credit.
Taylor's rule-based work and Woodford's framework may be considered different discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation research agenda shows how differences in resource allocation across firms and sectors can explain a large share of cross-country income and TFP differences. It combines microdata with growth accounting and has shifted both development and growth research. The impact is substantial, and the Hsieh-Klenow work on China and India is widely known.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow clearly carry the quantitative core. Restuccia is linked through the agriculture and misallocation work (Restuccia-Rogerson, Restuccia-Yang-Zhu), and Restuccia-Rogerson is not listed. Credit would be shared with Banerjee-Duflo and Restuccia-Rogerson, and this attribution is somewhat uncertain. I disclose that I am a frequent co-author of Klenow, which is a conflict that I do not adjudicate here. This ranking rests on the field's evidence and is deliberately not placed above the more mature candidates.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2008 to 2009 and have been replicated and critiqued in measurement terms. They are mature enough but continue to be debated on how much of misallocation is true distortion versus measurement error.
uncertainties: Conflict: frequent collaboration with Klenow. Not adjudicated.
Measurement-error critiques of the misallocation estimates.
Attribution with respect to Restuccia-Rogerson and other contributors.
The 2025 prize recognized growth theory, which may reduce the near-term appetite for another growth-related award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility using population-scale administrative data. It documents geographic variation and links it to neighborhood effects, and it has had unusual policy and public influence. The data and design innovations are a major methodological contribution to empirical economics.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader across the program. Hendren and Friedman are central co-authors on the Opportunity Insights projects, and Katz is a co-author on the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis. Attribution is clear for Chetty and less clear for the rest. Chetty also appears in the public-economics candidate B029, so the committee should not credit him twice.
assessment.maturity: Key papers date from 2014 to 2022. They are recent compared with typical prize timing, and the long-run replication and causal interpretation of neighborhood effects are still developing.
uncertainties: Recency and limited time for independent confirmation.
Causal interpretation of place-based variation.
Choice among Hendren, Friedman and Katz for credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators (Arellano-Bond, Arellano-Bover, Blundell-Bond) are among the most widely used tools in applied economics. They allow consistent estimation with lagged dependent variables and fixed effects in short panels, and they are used extensively in growth, finance, labor and IO work. The impact on empirical practice is very large, although the conceptual novelty is more incremental than in the top candidates.
assessment.attribution: The three names are well matched, with Arellano-Bond (1991) as the core, and Blundell-Bond (1998) and Arellano-Bover (1995) extending it. Credit also traces to Hansen's GMM, Holtz-Eakin-Newey-Rosen and Anderson-Hsiao, which are not listed. Blundell also appears in B033, so the committee should avoid a double count.
assessment.maturity: The core work is 25 to 35 years old and extremely well confirmed in use. Known weaknesses, such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments, are well documented.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is large enough relative to recent econometrics prizes (2021 and earlier).
Instrument proliferation and weak-instrument concerns in applications.
Prior contributions by Hansen, Anderson-Hsiao and others complicate credit.
